For <s>karmas</s> and their instruments such as the sacred thread are contrary to the realization of non-difference from the Supreme Self. <s>Karmas</s> are prescribed for the transmigrating being, and their instruments such as the sacred thread are likewise; not for one who sees non-difference from the Supreme Self. And by the mere vision of difference, one becomes other than That [Supreme Self]. // Upadeśasāhasrī II,1.30 //

body.text: yadi ca karmāṇi kartavyāni na nivartayiṣitāni karmasādhanāsambandhinaḥ karmanimittajātyāśramādyasambandhinaś ca paramātmana ātmanaivābhedapratipattiṃ nāvakṣyat "sa ātmā tat tvam asi" ityevamādibhir niścitarūpair vākyaiḥ, bhedapratipattinindāṃ ca nābhyadhāsyat "eṣa nityo mahimā brāhmaṇasya", "ananvāgataṃ puṇyenānanvāgataṃ pāpena", "atra steno 'stenaḥ" ityādinā // SamUpad_II,1.31 //
body.translated_text: And if [the <s>śruti</s>] had not intended to stop <s>karmas</s> and had not wished the realization of non-difference of the Self—who has no connection with the instruments of <s>karma</s> nor with caste, <s>āśrama</s>, and the like occasioned by <s>karma</s>—from the Supreme Self itself, it would not have taught [this identity] through definitive statements such as 'That is the Self; that thou art (<s>tat tvam asi</s>)' and the like; nor would it have added the censure of the perception of difference through passages such as 'This is the eternal greatness of the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>' [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23], 'Untouched by merit, untouched by sin' [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.22], 'Here a thief is no thief' [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.22], and the like. // Upadeśasāhasrī II,1.31 //

body.text: karmāsambandharūpatvaṃ karmanimittavarṇādyasambandharūpatāṃ [ca] nābhyadhāsyat, karmāṇi [ca] karmasādhanāni [ca] yajñopavītādīni yady aparitityājayiṣitāni / tasmāt sasādhanaṃ karma parityaktavyaṃ mumukṣuṇā paramātmābhedadarśanavirodhāt / ātmā ca para eveti pratipattavyo yathāśrutyuktalakṣaṇaḥ // SamUpad_II,1.32 //
body.translated_text: It would not have attributed to [the Self] the nature of having no connection with <s>karma</s>, nor the nature of having no connection with <s>varṇa</s> (caste) and the like occasioned by <s>karma</s>, if it had not intended <s>karmas</s> and the instruments of <s>karma</s> such as the sacred thread to be renounced. Therefore, <s>karma</s> together with its instruments must be renounced by one who seeks liberation (<s>mumukṣu</s>), because they are contrary to the vision of non-difference from the Supreme Self. And the Self is to be realized as none other than the Supreme, characterized as described by the <s>śruti</s>. // Upadeśasāhasrī II,1.32 //

body.text: sa yadi brūyāt -- bhagavan, dahyamāne chidyamāne vā dehe pratyakṣā vedanā, aśanāyādinimittaṃ ca pratyakṣaṃ duḥkhaṃ mama / paraś cātmā "apahatapāpmā vijaro vimṛtyur viśoko vijighatso 'pipāsaḥ" sarvasaṃsāradharmavivarjitaḥ śrūyate sarvaśrutiṣu smṛtiṣu ca / kathaṃ tadvilakṣaṇo 'nekasaṃsāradharmasaṃyuktaḥ paramātmānam ātmatvena māṃ ca saṃsāriṇaṃ paramātmatvenāgnim iva śītatvena pratipadyeyam / saṃsārī ca san sarvābhyudayaniḥśreyasasādhane 'dhikṛto 'bhyudayaniḥśreyasasādhanāni karmāṇi tatsādhanāni ca yajñopavītādīni kathaṃ parityajeyam iti // SamUpad_II,1.33 //
body.translated_text: If [the student] should say: 'Venerable Sir, when the body is being burned or cut, the sensation is directly perceived [by me]. And the suffering caused by hunger and the like is directly perceived as mine. But the Supreme Self is heard of in all <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s> texts as "free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger, free from thirst" [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5]—devoid of all properties of <s>saṃsāra</s>. How can I, who am characterized by the opposite [qualities] and endowed with numerous properties of <s>saṃsāra</s>, realize the Supreme Self as my Self, or myself, a transmigrating being, as the Supreme Self—like [attributing] coldness to fire? And being a transmigrating being, qualified for the means to both worldly prosperity (<s>abhyudaya</s>) and the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>), how can I renounce <s>karmas</s>, which are the means to prosperity and the highest good, and their instruments such as the sacred thread?' // Upadeśasāhasrī II,1.33 //

body.text: taṃ prati brūyāt -- yad avoco dahyamāne chidyamāne vā dehe pratyakṣā vedanopalabhyate mameti tad asat / kasmat / dahyamāne chidyamāna iva vrkṣa upalabdhur upalabhyamāne karmaṇi śarīre dāhacchedavedanāyā upalabhyamānatvād dāhādisamānāśrayaiva vedanā / yatra hi dāhaś chedo vā kriyate tatraiva vyapadiśati dāhādivedanāṃ loko na dāhādyupalabdharīti / katham / kva te vedaneti pṛṣṭaḥ śirasi me vedanorasy udara iti yatra dāhādis tatra vyapadiśati, nopalabdharīti / yady upalabdhari vedanā syād vedanānimittaṃ vā dāhacchedādi, vedanāśrayatvenopadiśed dāhādyāśrayāvat // SamUpad_II,1.34 //
body.translated_text: To him [the teacher] should say: 'What you said—that sensation is directly perceived as "mine" when the body is being burned or cut—that is incorrect. Why? Because when the body is being burned or cut, like a tree, [the sensation], being perceived in the body where the action [of burning or cutting] occurs—since it is perceived [there], sensation has the very same locus as the burning and the like. For the world speaks of the sensation of burning and the like at the place where the burning or cutting is done, not at the place of the perceiver. How so? When asked "Where is your pain?" one says "In my head," "In my chest," "In my stomach"—one points to where the burning and the like [occur], not to the perceiver. If the sensation belonged to the perceiver, or if the burning, cutting, and the like were caused by sensation, one would point to the perceiver as the locus of sensation, just as one points to the locus of the burning and the like.' // Upadeśasāhasrī II,1.34 //

body.text: svayaṃ ca nopalabhyeta cakṣurgatarūpavat / tasmād dāhacchedādisamānāśrayatvenopalabhyamānatvād dāhādivat karmabhūtaiva vedanā / bhāvarūpatvāc ca sāśrayā taṇḍulapākavat / vedanāsamānāśraya eva tatsaṃskāraḥ / smṛtisamānakāla evopalabhyamānatvāt / vedanāviṣayas tannimittaviṣayaś ca dveṣo 'pi saṃskārasamānāśraya eva / tathā coktam -- "rūpasaṃskāratulyādhī rāgadveṣau bhayaṃ ca yat / gṛhyate dhīśrayaṃ tasmāj jñātā śuddho 'bhayaḥ sadā" // SamUpad_II,1.35 //
body.translated_text: 'And [the perceiver] itself would not be perceived, like a form in the eye. Therefore, since sensation is perceived as having the same locus as burning, cutting, and the like, sensation is indeed an object [of perception], like burning and the like. And being a positive entity, it has a substratum, like the cooking of rice. The impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) [of sensation] has the very same substratum as the sensation. Because [the impression] is perceived only at the time of memory. And aversion, whose object is the sensation and its cause, also has the same substratum as the impression. As has been stated: "Attachment, aversion, and fear, which are afflictions comparable to form and mental impressions, are apprehended as depending on the intellect; therefore, the knower is always pure and fearless."' // Upadeśasāhasrī II,1.35 //

body.text: kimāśrayaḥ punā rūpādisaṃskārādaya iti / ucyate / yatra kāmādāyaḥ / kva punas te kāmādayaḥ / "kāmaḥ saṅkalpo vicikitsā" ityādiśruter buddhāv eva / tatraiva rūpādisaṃskāradayo 'pi, "kasmin nu rūpāṇi pratiṣṭhitānīti hṛdaye" iti śruteḥ / "kāmā ye 'sya hṛdi śritāḥ", "tīrṇo hi ", "asaṅgo hy ayam", "tad vā asyaitad aticchandāḥ" ityādiśrutiśatebhyaḥ, "avikāryo 'yam ucyate", "anāditvān nirguṇatvāt" ityādi -- icchādveṣādi ca kṣetrasyaiva viṣayasya dharmo nātmana iti -- smṛtibhyaś ca karmasthaivāśuddhir nātmasthā iti // SamUpad_II,1.36 //
body.translated_text: 'What is the substratum of form-impressions and the like?' It is said: 'Where desire and the like [reside].' 'And where do those desires and the like reside?' From the <s>śruti</s> 'desire, volition, doubt' [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3] and the like—in the intellect alone. Form-impressions and the like also [reside] there, from the <s>śruti</s> 'In what are forms established? In the heart' [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.20]. [And from <s>śruti</s> texts:] 'Desires that are lodged in the heart' [Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.3.14], 'He has crossed beyond' [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.1], 'For this one is unattached' [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15], 'That of his which transcends desire' [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21]—from hundreds of such <s>śruti</s> texts; and from <s>smṛti</s> texts such as 'He is said to be immutable' [Bhagavadgītā 2.25], 'Because of being beginningless and without qualities' [Bhagavadgītā 13.31]—desire, aversion, and the like are properties of the field (<s>kṣetra</s>), the object, not of the Self—and from <s>smṛtis</s> [it follows that] impurity belongs to <s>karma</s> alone, not to the Self. // Upadeśasāhasrī II,1.36 //

body.text: ato rūpādisaṃskārādyaśuddhisaṃbandhābhāvān na parasmād ātmano vilakṣaṇas tvam iti pratyakṣādivirodhābhāvād yuktaṃ para evātmāham iti pratipattum -- "tad ātmānam evāved [ahaṃ brahmāsmi]", "ekadhaivānudraṣṭavyam", "aham evādhastāt", "ātmaivādhastāt", "sarvam ātmānaṃ paśyet", "yatra tv asya sarvam ātmaiva", "idaṃ sarvaṃ yad ayam ātma", "sa eṣo ['kalaḥ ]", "anantaram abāhyam", "sabāhyābhyantaro hy ajaḥ", "brahmaivedam", "etayā dvārā prāpadyata", "prajñānasya nāmadheyāni", "satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma", "tasmād vā", "tat sṛṣṭvā tad evānuprāviśat", "eko devaḥ sarvabhūteṣu gūḍhaḥ", "aśarīraṃ śarīreṣu", "na jāyate mriyate", "svapnāntaṃ jāgaritāntam", "sa ma ātmeti vidyāt", "yas tu sarvāṇi bhūtāni", "tad ejati tan naijati", "venas tat paśyan", "tad evāgniḥ", "aham, manur abhavam sūryaś ca" "antaḥ praviṣṭaḥ śāstā janānām", "sad eva somya", "tat satyaṃ sa ātmā tat tvam asi" ityādiśrutibhyaḥ // SamUpad_II,1.37 //
body.translated_text: 'Therefore, since there is no connection with the impurities of form-impressions and the like, you are not different from the Supreme Self. And since there is no contradiction with perception and the like, it is proper to realize: "I am indeed the Supreme Self"—[as supported by <s>śruti</s> texts:] "He knew the Self: I am <s>Brahman</s>" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10], "It should be perceived as one alone" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.20], "I am indeed below" [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1], "The Self alone is below" [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2], "One should see everything as the Self" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23], "Where for him everything has become the Self alone" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15], "All this is this Self" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6], "That is without parts" [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2], "Without interior and without exterior" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19], "Without interior and exterior, indeed unborn" [Māṇḍūkya 7], "<s>Brahman</s> is indeed all this" [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11], "It entered through this door" [Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.3.12], "These are the names of consciousness" [Aitareya Upaniṣad 3.1.2], "<s>Brahman</s> is truth, knowledge, infinite" [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1], "From that indeed" [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1], "Having created it, it entered into that very thing" [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6], "The one God hidden in all beings" [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11], "The bodiless one among bodies" [Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.22], "It is not born, nor does it die" [Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18], "The dream state and the waking state" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7], "Let him know: this is my Self" [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.4], "He who [sees] all beings" [Īśā Upaniṣad 6], "It moves and it does not move" [Īśā Upaniṣad 5], "<s>Vena</s> saw that" [Ṛgveda 10.123.3], "That itself is fire" [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.1], "I was <s>Manu</s> and the sun" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10], "The inner controller, the ruler of all people" [Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.11], "Existence alone, O dear one" [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1], "That is the truth, that is the Self, that thou art (<s>tat tvam asi</s>)" [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7]'—and other such <s>śruti</s> texts. // Upadeśasāhasrī II,1.37 //

body.text: smṛtibhyaś ca -- "pūḥ prāṇinaḥ ... guhāśayasya", "ātmaiva devatāḥ", "navadvāre pure", "samaṃ sarveṣu bhūteṣu", "vidyāvinayasaṃpanne", "avibhaktaṃvibhakteṣu ", "vāsudevaḥ sarvam" ityādibhyaḥ, eka evātmā paraṃ brahma [sarva]saṃsāradharmavinirmuktas tvam iti siddham // SamUpad_II,1.38 //
body.translated_text: And from <s>smṛti</s> texts as well: 'The city of beings... dwelling in the cave [of the heart]' [Bhagavadgītā 5.13/15.17], 'The Self alone is all the deities' [Manusmṛti 12.119], 'In the city of nine gates' [Bhagavadgītā 5.13], 'Equal in all beings' [Bhagavadgītā 13.27], 'Endowed with learning and humility' [Bhagavadgītā 5.18], 'The undivided among the divided' [Bhagavadgītā 13.16], '<s>Vāsudeva</s> is everything' [Bhagavadgītā 7.19]—and from such texts, it is established: you are the one Self, the Supreme <s>Brahman</s>, free from all the properties of <s>saṃsāra</s>. // Upadeśasāhasrī II,1.38 //

body.text: sa yadi brūyāt -- yadi bhagavan "anantaro 'bāhyaḥ", "sabāhyābhyantaro hy ajaḥ", "kṛtsnaḥ prajñānaghana eva" saindhavaghanavad ātmā sarvamūrtibhedavarjita ākāśavad ekarasaḥ, kim idaṃ dṛśyate śrūyate vā sadhyaṃ sādhanaṃ [vā] sādhakaś ceti śrutismṛtilokaprasiddhaṃ vādiśatavipratipattiviṣaya iti // SamUpad_II,1.39 //
body.translated_text: If he should say: 'If, O Lord, [the Self is] "without interior or exterior," "unborn, with exterior and interior," "entirely a mass of consciousness" like a lump of salt, the Self is devoid of all distinctions of form, of uniform essence like space — then what is this that is seen or heard: the goal, the means, and the seeker, well-known in <s>śruti</s>, <s>smṛti</s>, and worldly [usage], and the subject of dispute among hundreds of debaters?' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.1.39 //

body.text: ācāryo brūyāt -- avidyākṛtam etad yad idaṃ dṛśyate śrūyate vā, paramārthatas tv eka evātmā avidyādrṣṭer anekavad avābhāsate, timiradṛṣṭyānekacandravat / "yatra vānyad iva syāt", "yatra hi dvaitam iva bhavati tad itara itaraṃ paśyati", "mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyum āpnoti", "atha yatrānyat paśyaty anyac chṛṇoty anyad vijānāti tad alpam, ... atha yad alpaṃ tan martyam", iti, "vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyam", ["anṛtam",] "anyo 'sāv anyo 'ham" iti bhedadarśananindopapatter avidyākṛtaṃ dvaitam "ekam evādvitīyam", "yatra tv asya", "ko mohaḥ kaḥ śokaḥ" ityādyekatvavidhiśrutibhyaś ceti // SamUpad_II,1.40 //
body.translated_text: The teacher should say: 'This that is seen or heard is the product of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). In ultimate reality, the Self alone is one; through the vision affected by <s>avidyā</s>, it appears as manifold, like the many moons [seen] through the vision affected by an eye-disease. [As the <s>śruti</s> says:] "Where there seems to be another," "Where there seems to be duality, there one sees the other," "He goes from death to death," "But where one sees something else, hears something else, knows something else — that is limited... and what is limited is mortal," and "A mere verbal expression, a modification, a name," ["unreal,"] "He is different, I am different" — since the censure of seeing difference is well-established, duality is the product of <s>avidyā</s>; and from <s>śruti</s> passages enjoining oneness such as "One alone, without a second," "But when for him," "What delusion, what sorrow?" and the like.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.1.40 //

body.text: yady evaṃ bhagavan, kimarthaṃ śrutyā sādhyasādhanādibheda ucyate utpattiḥ pralayaś ceti // SamUpad_II,1.41 //
body.translated_text: 'If so, O Lord, for what purpose does the <s>śruti</s> speak of the distinction of goal, means, and the like, and of origination and dissolution?' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.1.41 //

body.text: atrocyate -- avidyāvata upāttaśarīrādibhedasyeṣṭāniṣṭayoginam ātmānaṃ manyamānasya sādhanair eveṣṭāniṣṭaprāptiparihāropāyavivekam ajānata iṣṭaprāptiṃ cāniṣṭaparihāraṃ cecchataḥ śanais tadviṣayam ajñānaṃ nivartayati śāstraṃ na sādhyasādhanādibhedaṃ vidhatte / aniṣṭarūpaḥ saṃsāro hi sa iti tad bhedadṛṣṭim evāvidyāṃ saṃsāramūlam unmūlayati utpattipralayādyekatvopapattipradarśanena // SamUpad_II,1.42 //
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: 'For one who has <s>avidyā</s>, who identifies with the assumed body and the like, who considers the Self as connected with the desirable and undesirable, who does not know the discrimination of the means for attaining the desirable and avoiding the undesirable, and who desires the attainment of the desirable and the avoidance of the undesirable — scripture gradually removes the ignorance regarding those matters; it does not establish the distinction of goal, means, and the like. For <s>saṃsāra</s> is of the nature of what is undesirable; therefore [scripture] uproots the very vision of difference, which is <s>avidyā</s> and the root of <s>saṃsāra</s>, by demonstrating the logical establishment of oneness through [teachings on] origination, dissolution, and the like.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.1.42 //

body.text: avidyāyām unmūlitāyāṃ śrutismṛtinyāyebhyaḥ "anantaram abāhyam", "sabāhyābhyantaro hy ajaḥ" saindhavaghanavat "prajñānaghana eva", ekarasa ātmā ākāśavat paripūrṇa ity atraivaikā prajñā pratiṣṭhitā paramārthadarśino bhavati, na sādhyasādhanotpattipralayādibhedenāśuddhigandho 'py upapadyate // SamUpad_II,1.43 //
body.translated_text: 'When <s>avidyā</s> has been uprooted, from <s>śruti</s>, <s>smṛti</s>, and reasoning, [one knows that the Self is] "without interior or exterior," "unborn, with exterior and interior," like a lump of salt, "entirely a mass of consciousness," of uniform essence, all-pervading like space — in this alone does the single understanding of one who sees ultimate reality become established; not even a trace of impurity is possible through the distinction of goal, means, origination, dissolution, and the like.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.1.43 //

body.text: tac caitat paramārthadarśanaṃ pratipattum icchatā varṇāśramādyabhimānakṛtapāṅktarūpaputravittalokaiṣaṇādibhyo vyutthānaṃ kartavyam / samyakpratyayavirodhāt tadabhimānasya bhedadarśanapratiṣedhārthopapattiś copapadyate / na hy ekasminn ātmany asaṃsāritvabuddhau śāstranyāyotpāditāyāṃ tadviparītā buddhir bhavati / na hy agnau śītatvabuddhiḥ, śarīre vājarāmaraṇabuddhiḥ / tasmād avidyākāryatvāt sarvakarmaṇāṃ tatsādhanānāṃ ca yajñopavītādīnāṃ paramārthadarśananiṣṭhena tyāgaḥ kartavyaḥ // SamUpad_II,1.44 //
body.translated_text: 'One who wishes to attain this vision of ultimate reality must withdraw from the desires for lineage, form, sons, wealth, and worlds that arise from identification with <s>varṇa</s> (social class), <s>āśrama</s> (stage of life), and the like. The opposition to right understanding [makes this] logically sound, and the negation of seeing difference [also supports it]. For when the understanding of the Self as non-transmigrating, produced by scripture and reasoning, [arises] in the one Self, a contrary understanding does not arise — just as the understanding of coldness does not arise in fire, or the understanding of freedom from old age and death does not arise in the body. Therefore, since all actions and their means such as the sacred thread and the like are products of <s>avidyā</s>, their abandonment should be undertaken by one established in the vision of ultimate reality.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.1.44 //

body.text: iti śiṣyapratibodhana[vidhi]prakaraṇam // SamUpad_II,1 //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the chapter on the Method of Enlightening the Student (<s>Śiṣyapratibodhanavidhiprakaraṇa</s>). // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.1 //

body.text: sukham āsīnaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ brahmaniṣṭhaṃ kaścid brahmacārī janmamaraṇalakṣaṇāt saṃsārān nirviṇṇo mumukṣur vidhivad upasannaḥ papraccha -- bhagavan, katham ahaṃ saṃsārān mokṣiṣye / śarīrendriyaviṣayavedanāvān jāgarite duḥkham anubhavāmi tathā svapne 'nubhavāmi punaḥ punaḥ suṣuptipratipattyā viśramya / kim ayam eva mama svabhāvaḥ, kiṃ vānyasvabhāvasya sato naimittika iti / yadi svabhāvo na me mokṣāśā svabhāvasyāvarjanīyatvāt / atha naimittiko nimittaparihāre syān mokṣopapattiḥ // SamUpad_II,2.45 //
body.translated_text: A certain <s>brahmacārin</s> (student), disgusted with <s>saṃsāra</s> characterized by birth and death, desirous of liberation, having duly approached a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> who was comfortably seated, established in <s>Brahman</s>, asked: 'O Lord, how shall I be freed from <s>saṃsāra</s>? I experience suffering in the waking state, being endowed with body, senses, objects, and sensations; likewise I experience it in dreams, again and again resting through the attainment of deep sleep. Is this my very nature? Or is it contingent, while my [true] nature is something else? If it is my nature, there is no hope of liberation for me, since one's nature cannot be altered. But if it is contingent, then upon the removal of the cause, liberation would be logically possible.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.45 //

body.text: taṃ gurur uvāca -- śṛṇu vatsa, na tavāyaṃ svabhāvaḥ / naimittikaḥ // SamUpad_II,2.46 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said to him: 'Listen, dear child — this is not your nature. It is contingent.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.46 //

body.text: ity uktaḥ śiṣya uvāca -- kiṃ nimittam, kiṃ vā tasya nivartakam, ko vā mama svabhāvaḥ, yasmin nimitte nivartite naimittikābhāvo roganimittanivṛttāv iva rogī svabhāvaṃ pratipadyeyeti // SamUpad_II,2.47 //
body.translated_text: Being told this, the student said: 'What is the cause? What removes it? And what is my [true] nature? — so that when the cause is removed, the contingent [suffering] would be absent, and I would attain my own nature, just as a sick person [regains health] when the cause of the disease is removed.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.47 //

body.text: gurur uvāca -- avidyā nimittam, vidyā tasyā nivartikā, avidyāyāṃ nivṛttāyāṃ tannimittābhāvān mokṣyase janmamaraṇalakṣaṇāt saṃsārāt, svapnajāgradduḥkhaṃ ca nānubhaviṣyasīti // SamUpad_II,2.48 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said: '<s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance) is the cause; <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) is what removes it. When <s>avidyā</s> is removed, you will be freed from <s>saṃsāra</s> characterized by birth and death, due to the absence of its cause, and you will no longer experience the suffering of dreaming and waking.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.48 //

body.text: śiṣya uvāca -- kā sāvidyā, kiṃviṣayā vā, vidyā ca kāvidyānivartikā yayā svabhāvaṃ pratipadyeyeti // SamUpad_II,2.49 //
body.translated_text: The student said: 'What is that <s>avidyā</s>? What is its object? And what is the <s>vidyā</s> that removes <s>avidyā</s>, by which I would attain my own nature?' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.49 //

body.text: gurur uvāca-- tvaṃ paramātmānaṃ santam asaṃsāriṇaṃ saṃsāry aham asmīti viparītaṃ pratipadyase, akartāraṃ santaṃ karteti, abhoktāraṃ santaṃ bhokteti, vidyamānaṃ cāvidyamānam iti, iyam avidyā // SamUpad_II,2.50 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said: 'You, being the supreme Self, who is non-transmigrating, wrongly understand "I am transmigrating"; being a non-agent, [you wrongly understand] "I am an agent"; being a non-experiencer, "I am an experiencer"; being existent, "I am non-existent" — this is <s>avidyā</s>.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.50 //

body.text: śiṣya uvāca -- yady apy ahaṃ vidyamānas tathāpi na paramātmā / kartṛtvabhoktṛtvalakṣaṇaḥ saṃsāro mama svabhāvaḥ, pratyakṣādibhiḥ pramāṇair anubhūyamānatvāt / nāvidyānimittaḥ, avidyāyāḥ svātmaviṣayatvānupapatteḥ / avidyā nāmānyasminn anyadharmādhyāropaṇā / yathā prasiddhaṃ rajataṃ prasiddhāyāṃ śuktikāyām, yathā prasiddhaṃ puruṣaṃ sthāṇāv adhyāropayati, prasiddhaṃ vā sthāṇuṃ puruṣe / nāprasiddhaṃ prasiddhe, prasiddhaṃ vāprasiddhe / na cātmany anātmānam adhyāropayati, ātmano 'prasiddhatvāt / tathātmānam anātmani, ātmano 'prasiddhatvād eva // SamUpad_II,2.51 //
body.translated_text: The student said: 'Even though I am existent, still I am not the supreme Self. <s>Saṃsāra</s>, characterized by agency and experiencership, is my nature, since it is experienced through valid means of knowledge such as perception and the like. It is not caused by <s>avidyā</s>, because <s>avidyā</s> cannot logically have one's own Self as its object. For <s>avidyā</s> is the superimposition of the properties of one thing upon another — just as well-known silver is superimposed upon a well-known shell, or a well-known person upon a post, or a well-known post upon a person. [But] what is not known is not [superimposed] upon what is known, nor what is known upon what is not known. And one does not superimpose the non-self upon the Self, since the Self is not known. Likewise, the Self [is not superimposed] upon the non-self, precisely because the Self is not known.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.51 //

body.text: taṃ gurur uvāca -- na, vyabhicārāt / na hi vatsa, prasiddhaṃ prasiddha evādhyāropayatīti niyantuṃ śakyam / ātmany adhyāropaṇadarśanāt / gauro 'haṃ kṛṣṇo 'ham iti dehadharmasyāhaṃpratyayaviṣaya ātmany ahaṃpratyayaviṣayasya ca dehe 'yam aham asmīti // SamUpad_II,2.52 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said to him: 'No, because of deviation [from the rule]. Dear child, it cannot be laid down as a rule that what is known is superimposed only upon what is known. For superimposition upon the Self is observed: "I am fair, I am dark" — properties of the body are [superimposed] upon the Self which is the object of the I-notion, and the Self which is the object of the I-notion [is superimposed] upon the body in [the cognition] "this is I."' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.52 //

body.text: śiṣya āha -- prasiddha eva tarhy ātmāhaṃpratyayaviṣayatayā dehaś cāyam iti / tatraivaṃ sati prasiddhayor eva dehātmanor itaretarādhyāropaṇā[t] sthāṇupuruṣayoḥ śuktikārajatayor iva / tatra kaṃ viseṣam āśritya bhagavatoktaṃ prasiddhayor itaretarādhyāropaṇeti niyantuṃ na śakyata iti // SamUpad_II,2.53 //
body.translated_text: The student said: 'But then the Self is known, through being the object of the I-notion, and the body too [is known] as "this." In that case, there would be mutual superimposition of the body and the Self, both being known, just like [the cases of] a post and a person, or a shell and silver. In that regard, on what basis do you, the Lord, say that it cannot be laid down as a rule that the mutual superimposition is [only] of things that are [both] known?' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.53 //

body.text: gurur uvāca -- śṛṇu / satyaṃ prasiddhau dehātmānau na tu sthāṇupuruṣāv iva viviktapratyayaviṣayatayā sarvalokaprasiddhau / kathaṃ tarhi / nityam eva nirantarāviviktapratyayaviṣayatayā / na hy ayaṃ deho 'yam ātmeti viviktābhyāṃ pratyayābhyāṃ dehātmānau gṛhṇāti yataḥ kaścit / ata eva hi momuhyate loka ātmānātmaviṣaye, evam ātmā naivam ātmeti / imaṃ viśeṣam āśrityāvocaṃ naivaṃ śakyam iti // SamUpad_II,2.54 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said: 'Listen. It is true that the body and the Self are both known; but they are not known to everyone as having distinct cognitions, like a post and a person. How then? They are always and invariably known as the objects of undiscriminated cognitions. For no one apprehends the body and the Self through two distinct cognitions — "this is the body" and "this is the Self." It is precisely for this reason that the world is confused regarding the Self and the non-self — [thinking] "the Self is thus" or "the Self is not thus." It is with reference to this distinction that I said it cannot be [so] ruled.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.54 //

body.text: nanv avidyādhyāropitaṃ [yatra] yat tad asat [tatra] dṛṣṭam, yathā rajataṃ śuktikāyām, sthāṇau puruṣaḥ, rajjvāṃ sarpaḥ, ākāśe talamalinatvam ityādi / tathā dehātmanor api nityam evo nirantarāviviktapratyayatayetaretarādhyāropaṇā kṛtā syāt, tad itaretarayor nityam evāsattvaṃ syāt / yathā śuktikādiṣv avidyādhyāropitānāṃ rajatādīnāṃ nityam evātyantāsattvam, tadviparītānāṃ ca viparīteṣu, tadvad dehātmanor avidyayaivetaretarādhyāropaṇā kṛtā syāt / tatraivaṃ sati dehātmanor asattvaṃ prasajyeta / tac cāniṣṭam, vaināśikapakṣatvāt / atha tadviparyayeṇa deha ātmany avidyayādhyāropitaḥ, dehasyātmani sati asattvaṃ prasajyeta / tac cāniṣṭam, pratyakṣādivirodhāt / tasmād dehātmānau nāvidyayetaretarasminn adhyāropitau / kathaṃ tarhi / vaṃśastambhavan nityasaṃyuktau // SamUpad_II,2.55 //
body.translated_text: 'Now, wherever something superimposed through <s>avidyā</s> is [found] upon something [else], that [superimposed thing] is seen to be unreal there — as silver upon a shell, a person upon a post, a snake upon a rope, darkness and impurity upon the sky, and so on. Similarly, if there is mutual superimposition of the body and the Self through invariably undiscriminated cognition, then both would always be mutually unreal. Just as silver and the like superimposed through <s>avidyā</s> upon shells and the like are always absolutely unreal, and their opposites [are unreal] in their opposites — so too the mutual superimposition of the body and the Self would be done by <s>avidyā</s>. In that case, the unreality of both the body and the Self would follow — and that is undesirable, being the position of the nihilists. Or conversely, if the body is superimposed on the Self through <s>avidyā</s>, then the body, being [superimposed] on the Self, would be unreal — and that is undesirable, since it contradicts perception and the like. Therefore, the body and the Self are not mutually superimposed through <s>avidyā</s>. How then? They are eternally conjoined, like a bamboo and a pillar.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.55 //

body.text: na / anityatvaparārthatvaprasaṅgāt / saṃhatatvāt [parārthatvam anityatvaṃ ca] vaṃśastambhādivad eva / kiṃ ca yas tu parair dehena saṃhataḥ kalpita ātmā sa saṃhatatvāt parārthaḥ / tenāsaṃhataḥ paro 'nyo nityaḥ siddhas tāvat // SamUpad_II,2.56 //
body.translated_text: 'No. Because impermanence and serving another's purpose would follow. Since it is composite, [the Self would be] for another's purpose and impermanent, just like a bamboo and a pillar. Moreover, the Self that is imagined as conjoined with the body and the like, being composite, would serve another's purpose. Therefore, a distinct, other, eternal [Self], uncompounded with it, is at least established.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.56 //

body.text: tasyāsaṃhatasya dehe dehamātratayādhyāropitatvenāsattvānityatvādidoṣaprasaṅgo bhavati / tatra nirātmako deha iti vaināśikapakṣaprāptidoṣaḥ syāt // SamUpad_II,2.57 //
body.translated_text: 'Of that uncompounded [Self], since it is superimposed upon the body as being merely the body, the faults of unreality, impermanence, and the like would follow. In that case, the fault of reaching the nihilist position — that the body is without a Self — would arise.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.57 //

body.text: na / svata evātmana ākāśasyevāsaṃhatatvābhyupagamāt / sarveṇāsaṃhataḥ sann ātmeti na nirātmako dehādiḥ sarvaḥ syāt / yathā cākāśaṃ sarveṇāsaṃhatam iti sarvaṃ na nirākāśaṃ bhavati, evam / tasmān na vaināśikapakṣaprāptidoṣaḥ syāt // SamUpad_II,2.58 //
body.translated_text: 'No. Because the uncompoundedness of the Self is accepted as its very nature, like space. Being uncompounded with everything, the Self exists — therefore, everything including the body would not be without a Self. Just as space, being uncompounded with everything, [exists], and therefore nothing is without space — it is the same. Therefore, the fault of reaching the nihilist position does not arise.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.58 //

body.text: yat punar uktam, dehasyātmany asattve pratyakṣādivirodhaḥ syād iti / tan na / pratyakṣādibhir ātmani dehasya sattvānupalabdheḥ / na hy ātmani, kuṇḍe badaram, kṣīre sarpiḥ, tile tailam, bhittau citram iva ca, pratyakṣādibhir deha upalabhyate / tasmān na pratyakṣādivirodhaḥ // SamUpad_II,2.59 //
body.translated_text: 'As for the objection that if the body were unreal in the Self, there would be a contradiction with perception and the like — that is not so. Because the existence of the body in the Self is not apprehended through perception and the like. For the body is not perceived in the Self through perception and the like as a berry in a bowl, ghee in milk, oil in sesame seeds, or a painting on a wall. Therefore, there is no contradiction with perception and the like.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.59 //

body.text: kathaṃ tarhi pratyakṣādyaprasiddhātmani dehādhyāropaṇa, dehe cātmāropaṇā // SamUpad_II,2.60 //
body.translated_text: 'How then is there superimposition of the body upon the Self, which is not established through perception and the like, and superimposition of the Self upon the body?' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.60 //

body.text: nāyaṃ doṣaḥ / svabhāva[pra]siddhatvād ātmanaḥ / na hi kādācitkasiddhāv evādhyāropaṇā na nityasiddhāv iti niyantuṃ śakyam, ākāśe talamalādyadhyāropaṇadarśanāt // SamUpad_II,2.61 //
body.translated_text: 'This is not a fault. Because the Self is known through its own nature. For it cannot be laid down as a rule that superimposition occurs only upon what is occasionally established and not upon what is eternally established — since the superimposition of darkness and impurity upon space is observed.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.61 //

body.text: kiṃ bhagavan, dehātmanor itaretarādhyāropaṇā dehādisaṃghāṭakṛtāthavātmakṛteti // SamUpad_II,2.62 //
body.translated_text: 'O Lord, is the mutual superimposition of the body and the Self produced by the aggregate of body and the like, or by the Self?' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.62 //

body.text: gurur uvāca -- yadi dehādisaṃghātakṛtā, yadi vātmakṛtā, kiṃ tava syāt // SamUpad_II,2.63 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said: 'Whether it is produced by the aggregate of body and the like, or by the Self — what would that [matter] to you?' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.63 //

body.text: ity uktaḥ śiṣya āha -- yady ahaṃ dehādisaṃghātamātraḥ, tato mamācetanatvāt parārthatvam iti na matkṛtā dehātmanor itaretarādhyāropaṇā / athāham ātmā paro 'nyaḥ saṃghātāt, citimattvāt svārtha iti mayaiva citimatātmany adhyāropaṇā kriyate sarvānarthabījabhūtā // SamUpad_II,2.64 //
body.translated_text: Being told this, the student said: 'If I am merely the aggregate of body and the like, then, being unconscious, I serve another's purpose, and the mutual superimposition of body and Self is not produced by me. But if I am the Self, other [than] and distinct from the aggregate, being conscious, I serve my own purpose — and it is by me, the conscious Self, that the superimposition is made, which is the seed of all misfortune.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.64 //

body.text: ity ukto gurur uvāca -- anarthabījabhūtāṃ cen mithyādhyāropaṇāṃ jānīṣe, mā kārṣīs tarhi // SamUpad_II,2.65 //
body.translated_text: Being told this, the teacher said: 'If you know that the false superimposition is the seed of all misfortune, then do not make it!' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.65 //

body.text: naiva bhagavan, śaknomi na kartum / anyena kenacit prayukto 'haṃ na svatantra iti // SamUpad_II,2.66 //
body.translated_text: 'I cannot help making it, O Lord! I am impelled by something else; I am not independent.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.66 //

body.text: na tarhy acitimattvāt svārthas tvam / yena prayukto 'svatantraḥ pravartase, sa citimān svārthaḥ, saṃghāṭa eva tvam // SamUpad_II,2.67 //
body.translated_text: 'Then you are not conscious and do not serve your own purpose. That by which you are impelled and [made] dependent — that is conscious and serves its own purpose; you are merely the aggregate.' // <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s> II.2.67 //

body.text: yady acetano 'ham, kathaṃ sukhaduḥkhavedanāṃ bhavaduktaṃ ca jānāmi // SamUpad_II,2.68 //
body.translated_text: If I am insentient, how do I know the experience of pleasure and pain, and also what you have said? // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.68 //

body.text: gurur uvāca -- kiṃ sukhaduḥkhavedanāyā maduktāc cānyas tvaṃ kiṃ vānanya eveti // SamUpad_II,2.69 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said: 'Are you different from the experience of pleasure and pain and from what I have said, or are you not different at all?' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.69 //

body.text: śiṣya uvāca -- nāhaṃ tāvad ananyaḥ / kasmāt / yasmāt tadubhayaṃ karmabhūtaṃ gaṭādim iva jānāmi / yadi ananyo 'ham, tena tadubhayaṃ na jānīyām, kiṃ tu jānāmi, tasmād anyaḥ / sukhaduḥkhavedanāvikriyā ca svārthaiva prāpnoti, tvaduktaṃ ca syāt, ananyatve, na ca tayoḥ svārthatā yuktā / na hi candanakaṇṭakakṛte sukhaduḥkhe candanakaṇṭakārthe, ghaṭopayogo vā ghaṭārthaḥ / tasmāt tadvijñātur mama candanādikṛto 'rthaḥ / ahaṃ hi tato 'nyaḥ samastam arthaṃ jānāmi buddhyārūḍham // SamUpad_II,2.70 //
body.translated_text: The disciple said: 'I am certainly not non-different from them. Why? Because I know both of those as objects, like a pot and the like. If I were non-different from them, I would not know them; but since I do know them, therefore I am different. Moreover, if there were non-difference, the modification consisting of the experience of pleasure and pain would be for its own sake, and so would your statement—but self-purposiveness for those two is not reasonable. For the pleasure and pain caused by sandalwood and thorns do not exist for the sake of sandalwood and thorns, nor is the use of a pot for the pot's own sake. Therefore, the purpose of sandalwood and the like pertains to me, the knower of them. For I, being different from them, know all objects that have arisen in the intellect.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.70 //

body.text: taṃ gurur uvāca -- evaṃ tarhi svārthas tvaṃ citimattvān na pareṇa prayujyase / na hi citimān paratantraḥ pareṇa prayujyate, citimataś citimadarthatvānupapatteḥ, samatvāt, prakāśayor iva / nāpy acitimadarthatvaṃ citimato bhavati, acitimato 'citimattvād eva svārthasaṃbandhānupapatteḥ / nāpy acitimator anyonyārthatvaṃ dṛṣṭam / na hi kāṣṭhakuḍye 'nyonyārthaṃ kurvāte // SamUpad_II,2.71 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said to him: 'If so, then you exist for your own purpose; since you possess consciousness, you are not employed by another. For a conscious being, being independent, is not employed by another, since it is impossible for a conscious being to exist for the sake of another conscious being, on account of their equality—like two lights. Nor does a conscious being exist for the sake of an insentient thing, since an insentient thing, being devoid of consciousness, cannot have a self-purposive relation. Nor is mutual purposiveness among insentient things observed—for a piece of wood and a wall do not serve each other's purpose.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.71 //

body.text: nanu citimattve same 'pi bhṛtyasvāminor anyonyārthatvaṃ dṛṣṭam // SamUpad_II,2.72 //
body.translated_text: The disciple objected: 'But is not mutual purposiveness observed between a servant and a master, even though both are equally conscious?' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.72 //

body.text: naivam, agner uṣṇaprakāśavat tava citimattvasya vivakṣitatvāt / darśitaś ca dṛṣṭāntaḥ prakāśayor iveti / tatraivaṃ sati svabuddhyārūḍham eva sarvam upalabhase 'gnyuṣṇaprakāśatulyena kūṭasthanityacaitanyasvarūpeṇa / yadi caivam ātmanaḥ sarvadā nirviśeṣatvam abhyupagacchasi / kim ity ūcivān, suṣupte viśramya viśramya jāgratsvapnayor duḥkham anubhavāmi / kim ayam eva mama svabhāvaḥ, kiṃ vā naimittika iti ca / kim asau vyāmoho 'pagataḥ, kiṃ vā na // SamUpad_II,2.73 //
body.translated_text: The teacher replied: 'Not so, because the consciousness intended here in your case is like the heat and light of fire—inseparable from your nature. And the example has been shown: "like two lights." This being so, you perceive everything that has arisen in your own intellect by your nature, which is immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>), eternal consciousness, comparable to the heat and light of fire. And if you thus accept that the Self is always without distinctions, then why did you say: "Having rested in deep sleep, I experience suffering in waking and dreaming; is this my very nature, or is it caused by something?" Has that delusion departed, or not?' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.73 //

body.text: ity uktaḥ śiṣya uvāca -- bhagavan, apagatas tvatprasādād vyāmohaḥ, kiṃ tu mama kūṭasthatāyāṃ saṃśayaḥ / katham / śabdādīnāṃ svataḥsiddhir nāsti, acetanatvāt / śabdādyākārapratyayotpattes tu teṣām / pratyayānām itaretaravyāvṛttaviśeṣaṇānāṃ nīlapītādyākāravatāṃ svataḥsiddhyasaṃbhavāt / tasmād bāhyākāranimittatvaṃ gamyata iti bāhyākāravacchabdādyākāratvasiddhiḥ / tathā pratyayānām apy ahaṃpratyayālambanavastubhedānāṃ saṃhatatvād acaitanyopapatteḥ svārthatvāsaṃbhavāt svarūpavyatiriktagrāhakagrāhyatvena siddhiḥ śabdādivad eva / asaṃhatatve sati caitanyātmakatvāt svārtho 'py ahaṃ pratyayānāṃ nīlapītādyākārāṇām upalabdheti vikriyāvān eva, kūṭastha iti saṃśayaḥ // SamUpad_II,2.74 //
body.translated_text: Thus addressed, the disciple said: 'Venerable sir, by your grace the delusion has departed. However, I have a doubt about my immutability (<s>kūṭastha</s>). How so? Sound and other objects have no self-established existence, being insentient. Their existence is established from the arising of cognitions having the form of sound and the like. And since cognitions—which are characterized by distinct forms such as blue, yellow, and the like, mutually differentiated—cannot have self-established existence either, their dependence on external forms is understood, and thus the existence of sound and the like having external forms is established. Likewise, cognitions too—which differ in their objects such as the substrate of the I-cognition, and which are composite, and hence reasonably insentient, and therefore cannot exist for their own sake—are established through a knower and knowable distinct from their own nature, just like sound and the like. Yet if I am uncomposite, being of the nature of consciousness, and thus exist for my own purpose, then I, the perceiver of cognitions having the forms of blue, yellow, and the like, undergo modification—hence the doubt: am I immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>) or not?' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.74 //

body.text: taṃ gurur uvāca -- na yuktas tava saṃśayaḥ / yatas teṣāṃ pratyayānāṃ niyamenāśeṣata upalabdher evāpariṇāmitvāt kūṭasthatvasiddhau niścayahetum evāśeṣacittapracāropalabdhiṃ saṃśayahetum āttha / yadi hi tava pariṇāmitvaṃ syāt, aśeṣasvaviṣayacittapracāropalabdhir na syāt, cittasyeva svaviṣaye yathā cendriyāṇāṃ svaviṣayeṣu / na ca tathātmanas tava svaviṣayaikadeśopalabdhiḥ / ataḥ kūṭasthataiva taveti // SamUpad_II,2.75 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said to him: 'Your doubt is not justified. For the very perception—without exception and without remainder—of all those cognitions, since that perception is unchanging, establishes your immutability (<s>kūṭastha</s>). Yet you cite as the ground for doubt the very perception of all mental operations, which is actually the ground for certainty. For if you were subject to modification, you would not perceive all mental operations within your own domain—just as the mind perceives only in its own domain, and just as the senses perceive only in their respective domains. But you do not perceive only a portion of your own domain. Therefore, immutability alone is yours.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.75 //

body.text: tatrāha -- upalabdhir nāma dhātvartho vikriyaiva, upalabdhuḥ kūṭasth[ātm]atā ceti viruddham // SamUpad_II,2.76 //
body.translated_text: To this the disciple said: 'Apprehension (<s>upalabdhi</s>) is a verbal root-meaning, hence a modification; and that the apprehender is immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>)—this is contradictory.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.76 //

body.text: na / dhātvarthavikriyāyām upalabdhyupacārāt / yo hi bauddhaḥ pratyayaḥ sa dhātvartho vikriyātmaka ātmana upalabdhyābhāsaphalāvasāna ity upalabdhiśabdenopacaryate / yathā chidikriyā dvaidhībhāvaphalāvasāneti dhātvarthatvenopacaryate, tadvat // SamUpad_II,2.77 //
body.translated_text: The teacher replied: 'Not so, because the term "apprehension" is used figuratively for the modification that is the verbal root-meaning. For the intellectual cognition (<s>bauddha pratyaya</s>) is the verbal root-meaning, being a modification by nature, and it terminates in the result of a semblance of the Self's apprehension—hence it is figuratively called "apprehension." Just as the action of cutting is figuratively described as the verbal root-meaning because it terminates in the result of splitting in two—so too here.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.77 //

body.text: ity uktaḥ śiṣya āha -- nanu bhagavan, mama kūṭasthatvapratipādanaṃ praty asamartho dṛṣṭāntaḥ / katham / chidiś chedyavikriyāvasānopacaryate yathā dhātvarthatvena, tathopalabdhiśabdopacarito 'pi dhātvartho bauddhapratyaya ātmana upalabdhivikriyāvasānaś cen nātmanaḥ kūṭasthatāṃ pratipādayituṃ samarthaḥ // SamUpad_II,2.78 //
body.translated_text: Thus addressed, the disciple said: 'But, venerable sir, this example is insufficient to establish my immutability. How so? Just as the action of cutting is figuratively described as the verbal root-meaning because it terminates in the modification of the thing cut, so too, if the intellectual cognition figuratively called "apprehension," being a verbal root-meaning, terminates in the modification of apprehension in the Self—then it is not capable of establishing the immutability of the Self.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.78 //

body.text: gurur uvāca -- satyam evaṃ syāt, yady upalabdhyupalabdhror viśeṣaḥ / nityopalabdhimātra eva hy upalabdhā / na tu tārkikasamaya ivānyopalabdhir anya ca upalabdhā ca // SamUpad_II,2.79 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said: 'That would indeed be true if there were a distinction between apprehension and the apprehender. But the apprehender is nothing but eternal apprehension itself. It is not the case, as the logicians (<s>tārkikas</s>) hold, that apprehension is one thing and the apprehender is another.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.79 //

body.text: nanūpalabdhiphalāvasāno dhātvarthaḥ katham iti // SamUpad_II,2.80 //
body.translated_text: 'But how can the verbal root-meaning terminate in the result of apprehension?' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.80 //

body.text: ucyate -- śṛṇu, upalabdhyābhāsaphalāvasāna ity uktam, kiṃ na śrutaṃ tvayā / na tv ātmano vikriyotpādanāvasāna iti mayoktam // SamUpad_II,2.81 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said: 'Listen—it was stated that it terminates in the result of a semblance of apprehension. Did you not hear that? I did not say that it terminates in producing a modification in the Self.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.81 //

body.text: śiṣya āha -- kathaṃ tarhi kūṭasthe mayy aśeṣasvaviṣayacittapracāropalabdhṛtvam ity āttha // SamUpad_II,2.82 //
body.translated_text: The disciple said: 'How then do you say that I, who am immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>), am the perceiver of all mental operations within my own domain?' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.82 //

body.text: taṃ gurur uvāca -- satyam evāvocam, tenaiva kūṭasthatām abruvaṃ tava // SamUpad_II,2.83 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said to him: 'I did indeed say exactly that, and by that very statement I declared your immutability.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.83 //

body.text: yady evaṃ bhagavan, kūṭasthanityopalabdhisvarūpe mayi śabdādyākārabauddhapratyayeṣu matsvarūpopalabdhyābhāsaphalāvasānavatsūtpadyāmaneṣu, kas tv aparādho mama // SamUpad_II,2.84 //
body.translated_text: 'If so, venerable sir, when intellectual cognitions having the forms of sound and the like arise in me—whose nature is immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>), eternal apprehension—and their result terminates in a semblance of my own apprehension, then what fault is there in me?' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.84 //

body.text: satyam, nāsty aparādhaḥ, kiṃ tv avidyāmātras tu aparādha iti prāg evāvocam // SamUpad_II,2.85 //
body.translated_text: 'True, there is no fault. But I have already said that the fault is nothing but mere <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.85 //

body.text: yadi bhagavan, suṣupta iva mama vikriyā nāsti, kathaṃ svapnajāgarite // SamUpad_II,2.86 //
body.translated_text: 'If, venerable sir, I have no modification as in deep sleep, then how is it in dreaming and waking?' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.86 //

body.text: taṃ gurur uvāca -- kiṃ tv anubhūyete tvayā sa[n]tatam // SamUpad_II,2.87 //
body.translated_text: The teacher said to him: 'But are those states experienced by you continuously?' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.87 //

body.text: bāḍham anubhavāmi, kiṃ tu vicchidya vicchidya na tu santatam // SamUpad_II,2.88 //
body.translated_text: 'Yes, I do experience them, but intermittently—not continuously.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.88 //

body.text: taṃ
body.translated_text: The teacher said: 'Then these are adventitious and not intrinsic to you. If they were intrinsic to you, they would be self-established and continuous, like the nature of consciousness itself. Moreover, dreaming and waking are not intrinsic to you, since they are variable, like clothing and the like. For that which is the essential nature of something is never observed to deviate from it. But dreaming and waking deviate from mere consciousness. If the essential nature in deep sleep were to deviate, then it would be destroyed or non-existent, and thus would be sublatable—since among adventitious things that lack the properties of the Self, both [outcomes]

body.text: gurur uvāca -- āgantuke tv ete na tavātmabhūte / yadi tavātmabhūte caitanyasvarūpavat svataḥsiddhe santate eva syātām / kiṃ ca svapnajāgarite na tavātmabhūte, vyabhicāritvāt, vastrādivat / na hi yasya yat svarūpaṃ tat tadvyabhicāri dṛṣṭam / svapnajāgarite tu caitanyamātratvād vyabhicarataḥ / suṣupte cet svarūpaṃ vyabhicaret, tan naṣṭaṃ nāstīti vā bādhyam eva syāt, āgantukānām ataddharmāṇām ubhayātmakatvadarśanāt, yathā dhanavastrādīnāṃ nāśo dṛṣṭaḥ, svapnabhrāntilabdhānāṃ tv abhāvo dṛṣṭaḥ // SamUpad_II,2.89 //
body.translated_text: are observed: the destruction of wealth, clothing, and the like is observed, and the non-existence of things obtained in dreams and illusions is observed.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.89 //

body.text: nanv evaṃ bhagavan, caitanyasvarūpam apy āgantukaṃ prāptam, svapnajāgaritayor iva suṣupte 'nupalabdheḥ / acaitanyasvarūpo vā syām aham // SamUpad_II,2.90 //
body.translated_text: 'But, venerable sir, in that case, the nature of consciousness too would turn out to be adventitious, since it is not perceived in deep sleep, just as in dreaming and waking. Or I would be of an insentient nature.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.90 //

body.text: na, paśya, tadanupapatteḥ / caitanyasvarūpaṃ ced āgantukaṃ paśyasi, paśya / naitad varśaśatenāpy upapattyā kalpayituṃ śaknumo vayam, anyo vācaitanyo 'pi / [tasya] saṃhatatvāt pārārthyam anekatvaṃ nāśitvaṃ ca na kenacid upapattyā vārayituṃ śakyam / asvārthasya svataḥsiddhyabhāvād ity avocāma / caitanyasvarūpasya tv ātmanaḥ svataḥsiddher anyānapekṣatvaṃ na kenacid vārayituṃ śakyam, avyabhicārāt // SamUpad_II,2.91 //
body.translated_text: The teacher replied: 'Not so—consider, for that is untenable. If you consider the nature of consciousness to be adventitious, then consider this: neither we nor anyone else, even in a hundred years, can establish this through reasoning. Nor can anyone else who is insentient do so. Being composite, its purposiveness for another, its plurality, and its destructibility cannot be prevented by any reasoning—for we have said that what is not for its own sake cannot be self-established. But the self-establishment of the Self whose nature is consciousness, and its independence from anything else, cannot be prevented by anyone, due to its invariability.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.91 //

body.text: nanu vyabhicāro darśito mayā suṣupte na paśyāmīti // SamUpad_II,2.92 //
body.translated_text: 'But I have demonstrated a deviation of consciousness in deep sleep—"I do not see anything."' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.92 //

body.text: na / vyāhatatvāt / kathaṃ vyāghātaḥ / paśyatas tava na paśyāmīti vyāhataṃ vacanam / na hi kadācid bhagavan, suṣupte mayā caitanyam anyad vā kiṃcid dṛṣṭam / paśyaṃs tarhi suṣupte tvam / yasmād dṛṣṭam eva pratiṣedhasi, na dṛṣṭim / yā tava dṛṣṭis tac caitanyam iti mayoktam / yayā tvaṃ vidyamānayā na kiṃcid dṛṣṭam iti pratiṣedhasi, sā dṛṣṭis tac caitanyam / tarhi sarvatrāvyabhicārāt kūṭasthanityatvaṃ siddhaṃ svata eva, na pramāṇāpekṣam / svataḥsiddhasya hi pramātur anyasya prameyasya paricchittiṃ prati pramāṇāpekṣā / yā tv anyā nityā paricchittir apekṣyate 'nyasyāparicchittirūpasya paricchedāya, sā hi nityaiva kūṭasthā svayaṃjyotiḥsvabhāvā / ātmani pramāṇatve pramātṛtve vā na tāṃ prati pramāṇāpekṣā, tatsvabhāvatvāt / yathā prakāśanam uṣṇatvaṃ vā lohodakādiṣu parato 'pekṣyate 'gnyādityādibhyaḥ, atatsvabhāvatvāt, nāgnyādityādīnāṃ tadapekṣā, sarvadā tatsvabhāvatvāt // SamUpad_II,2.93 //
body.translated_text: The teacher replied: 'Not so, because it is self-contradictory. How is there a contradiction? Your statement "I do not see" is contradictory, since you are a seer. "But, venerable sir, I did not see consciousness or anything else in deep sleep." Yet you were seeing in deep sleep—since you negate only what was seen, not the seeing itself. Your seeing—that is consciousness, as I have stated. That seeing, by which, while it exists, you negate saying "I did not see anything"—that seeing is consciousness. Therefore, since it never deviates anywhere, its immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>), eternal nature is established of itself, without depending on any means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). For it is the self-established knower that requires a means of knowledge for the determination of some other knowable thing. But that other, eternal determination which is required for the determination of what is of a nature other than determination—that is indeed eternally immutable, self-luminous by nature. For the Self, whether as means of knowledge or as knower, no means of knowledge is required, since that is its very nature. Just as illumination or heat is required in iron, water, and the like from fire and the sun, since that is not their own nature; but for fire and the sun there is no such requirement, since it is always their own nature.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.93 //

body.text: anityatva eva pramā syān na nityatva iti cet // SamUpad_II,2.94 //
body.translated_text: 'But valid knowledge (<s>pramā</s>) would exist only in what is impermanent, not in what is eternal.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.94 //

body.text: na / avagater nityatvānityatvayor viśeṣānupapatteḥ / na hy avagateḥ pramātve 'nityāvagatiḥ pramā na nityeti viśeṣo 'vagamyate // SamUpad_II,2.95 //
body.translated_text: The teacher replied: 'Not so, because there is no distinction between permanence and impermanence for awareness itself. For when awareness serves as a means of valid knowledge, no distinction can be apprehended that impermanent awareness is valid knowledge while eternal awareness is not.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.95 //

body.text: nityāyāṃ pramātur apekṣābhāvaḥ / anityāyāṃ tu yatnāntaritatvād avagatir apekṣyata iti viśeṣaṃ syād iti cet // SamUpad_II,2.96 //
body.translated_text: 'In the case of eternal awareness, there is no need for a knower. But in the case of impermanent awareness, since it is mediated by effort, awareness is required—this would be the distinction.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.96 //

body.text: siddhā tarhy ātmanaḥ pramātuḥ svataḥsiddhiḥ, pranāṇanirapekṣatayaiveti // SamUpad_II,2.97 //
body.translated_text: 'Then the self-establishment of the Self as knower is proven, precisely by its independence from any means of valid knowledge.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.97 //

body.text: abhāve 'py apekṣābhāvaḥ, nityatvād iti cet / na / avagater evātmani sadbhāvād iti parihṛtam etat // SamUpad_II,2.98 //
body.translated_text: 'Even in non-existence there would be no need for a means of knowledge, since it is eternal.' The teacher replied: 'Not so, because awareness exists in the Self itself—this has already been addressed.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.98 //

body.text: pramātuś cet pramāṇāpekṣāsiddhiḥ, kasya pramitsā syāt / yasya pramitsā sa eva pramātābhyupagamyate / tadīyā ca pramitsā prameyaviṣayaiva, na pramātṛviṣayā / pramātṛviṣayatve 'navasthāprasaṅgāt pramātus tadicchāyāś ca, tasyāpy anyaḥ pramātā, tasyāpy anya iti / evam evecchāyāḥ pramātṛviṣayatve / pramātur ātmano 'vyavahitatvāc ca prameyatvanupapattiḥ / loke hi prameyaṃ nāma pramātur icchāsmṛtiprayatnapramāṇajanmavyavahitaṃ siddhyati, nānyathāvagatiḥ prameyaviṣayā dṛṣṭā / na ca pramātuḥ pramātā svasya svayam eva kenacid vyavahitaḥ kalpayituṃ śakya icchādīnām anyatamenāpi / smṛtiś ca smartavyaviṣayā, na smartṛviṣayā / tathecchāyā iṣṭaviṣayatvam eva, necchāvadviṣayatvam / smartricchāvadviṣayatve 'pi hy ubhayor anavasthā pūrvavad aparihāryā syāt // SamUpad_II,2.99 //
body.translated_text: 'If the independence of the knower from means of valid knowledge is established, then whose desire to know would there be? He who has the desire to know is himself acknowledged as the knower. And his desire to know has as its object only the knowable, not the knower. For if it had the knower as its object, there would be an infinite regress of the knower and of its desire—another knower would be needed for that one, and yet another for that, and so on. The same applies if the desire to know had the knower as its object. And since the Self as knower is unmediated, it cannot be a knowable object. For in the world, something called "knowable" is established only as mediated from the knower by desire, memory, effort, and means of knowledge—no cognition of a knowable has been observed otherwise. Nor can the knower be imagined to be mediated from itself by any of these—desire and the rest. And memory has as its object only the remembered, not the rememberer. Likewise, desire has as its object only the desired, not the desirer. Even if the rememberer and the desirer were made objects, the infinite regress would be unavoidable for both, as before.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.99 //

body.text: nanu pramātṛviṣayāvagatyanutpattāv anavagata eva pramātā syād iti cet // SamUpad_II,2.100 //
body.translated_text: [Objection:] If the awareness whose content is the knower and the object does not arise, then the knower would remain simply unknown. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.100 //

body.text: na, avagantur avagater avagantavyaviṣayatvāt / avagantṛviṣayatve cānavasthā pūrvavat syāt / avagatiś cātmani kūṭasthanityātmajyotir anyato 'napekṣaiva siddhā, agnyādityādyuṣṇaprakāśavad iti pūrvam eva prasādhitam / avagateś caitanyātmajyotiṣaḥ svātmany anityatva ātmanaḥ svārthatānupapattiḥ, kāryakaraṇa[saṃghāta]vat saṃhatatvāt pārārthyaṃ doṣavattvaṃ cāvocāma / katham / caitanyātmajyotiṣaḥ svātmany anityatve smṛtyādivyavadhānāt saṃhatatvam / tataś ca tasya caitanyajyotiṣaḥ prāg utpatteḥ pradhvaṃsāc cordhvam ātmany evābhāvāt, cakṣurādīnām iva saṃhatatvāt, pārārthyaṃ syāt / yadā ca tad utpannam ātmani vidyate, na tadātmanaḥ svārthatvam / tadbhāvābhāvāpekṣā hy ātmānātmanoḥ svārthatvaparārthatvasiddhiḥ / tasmād ātmano 'nyanirapekṣam eva nityacaitanyajyotiṣṭvaṃ siddham // SamUpad_II,2.101 //
body.translated_text: No, because the awareness of the knower has as its object what is to be known [not the knower itself]. And if it were directed at the knower, there would be an infinite regress as before. And awareness, which is the self-luminous light of the immutable, eternal Self, is established as independent of anything else — like the heat and light of fire and the sun — this was already proven earlier. Moreover, if awareness, which is the light of the consciousness-Self, were non-eternal in its own Self, it would be impossible for the Self to exist for its own sake; we said that because it would be composite like the aggregate of effect and instruments, it would exist for another's sake and would be defective. How so? If the light of consciousness-Self were non-eternal in its own Self, it would be composite due to the interruption by memory and the like. And therefore, that light of consciousness, before its arising and after its destruction, would not exist in the Self; just like the eyes and the like, being composite, it would exist for another's sake. And when it does arise and exist in the Self, even then it is not for the Self's own sake. For the establishment of existing-for-one's-own-sake and existing-for-another's-sake, regarding Self and non-Self, depends on the presence and absence of that [consciousness]. Therefore, the eternal nature of the Self as the light of consciousness, independent of anything else, is established. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.101 //

body.text: nanv evaṃ sati, asati pramātṛtve kathaṃ pramātuḥ pramātṛtvam // SamUpad_II,2.102 //
body.translated_text: [Objection:] If so, when there is no knower-ship, how is the knower a knower? // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.102 //

body.text: ucyate -- pramāyā nityatve 'nityatve ca rūpaviśeṣābhāvāt / avagatir hi pramā / tasyāḥ smṛtīcchādipūrvikāyā anityāyaḥ kūṭasthanityāyā vā, na [sva]rūpaviśeṣo vidyate / yathā dhātvarthasya tiṣṭhatyādeḥ phalasya gatyādipūrvakasyānityasyāpūrvasya nityasya vā, rūpaviśeṣo nāstīti tulyo vyapadeśo dṛṣṭaḥ -- tiṣṭhanti manuṣyāḥ, tiṣṭhanti parvatā ityādi / tathā nityāvagatisvarūpe 'pi pramātari pramātṛtvavyapadeśo na virudhyate, phalasāmānyād iti // SamUpad_II,2.103 //
body.translated_text: It is said: Whether knowledge (<s>pramā</s>) is eternal or non-eternal, there is no difference in its essential nature. For awareness is knowledge. Whether it is non-eternal, preceded by memory, desire, and the like, or whether it is immutable and eternal — there is no difference in essential nature. Just as, for the meaning of verbal roots like 'stands' (<s>tiṣṭhati</s>), the result — whether preceded by movement and the like, non-eternal, unprecedented, or eternal — has no difference in form, and the same designation is observed: 'People stand,' 'Mountains stand,' and so forth. Likewise, even for the knower whose essential nature is eternal awareness, the designation 'knower' is not contradictory, due to the commonality of result. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.103 //

body.text: atrāha śiṣyaḥ -- nityāvagatisvarūpasyātmano 'vikriyatvāt kāryakaraṇair asaṃhatya, takṣādīnām iva vāsyādibhiḥ, kartṛtvaṃ nopapadyate, asaṃhatasvabhāvasya ca kāryakaraṇopādāne 'navasthā prasajyeta / takṣādīnāṃ tu kāryakaraṇair nityam eva saṃhatatvam iti vāsyādyupādāne nānavasthā syād iti // SamUpad_II,2.104 //
body.translated_text: Here the disciple says: Since the Self, whose essential nature is eternal awareness, is without modification, agency is not possible for it without combining with the body-and-sense apparatus — just as for carpenters and the like with an adze and other tools. And for one whose nature is non-composite, if instruments are to be taken up, there would be an infinite regress. But for carpenters and the like, since they are always composite with instruments, there is no infinite regress in taking up an adze and the like. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.104 //

body.text: iha tv asaṃhatasvabhāvasya karaṇānupādāne kartṛtvaṃ nopapadyata iti karaṇam upādeyam, tadupādānam api vikriyaiveti tatkartṛtve karaṇāntaram upādeyam, tadupādāne 'py anyad iti pramātuḥ svātantrye 'navasthāparihāryā syāt / na ca kriyaivātmānaṃ kārayati, anirvartitāyāḥ svarūpābhāvāt / athānyad ātmānam upetya kriyāṃ kārayatīti cet / na / anyasya svataḥsiddhatvāviṣayatvādyanupapatteḥ / na hy ātmano 'nyad acetanaṃ vastu svapramāṇakaṃ dṛṣṭam / śabdādisarvam evāvagatiphalāvasānapratyayapramitaṃ siddhaṃ syāt / avagatiś ced ātmano 'nyasya syāt, so 'py ātmaivāsaṃhataḥ svārthaḥ syān na parārthaḥ / na ca dehendriyaviṣayāṇāṃ svārthatām avagantuṃ śaknumo 'vagatyavasānapratyayāpekṣasiddhidarśanāt // SamUpad_II,2.105 //
body.translated_text: But here, for one whose nature is non-composite, if without taking up an instrument agency is impossible, then an instrument must be taken up; but taking it up is itself an action, so for agency in that, another instrument must be taken up; and for taking that up, yet another — thus, if the knower is independent, an infinite regress would be unavoidable. Nor does the action itself cause the Self [to act], since before it is accomplished, its own nature does not exist. If [you say] something else, approaching the Self, causes the action — no, because it is impossible for anything other [than the Self] to be self-established, to be non-objectal, and so forth. For no unconscious thing other than the Self is seen to have its own means of valid knowledge. Everything — sound and all the rest — would be established through cognitions that terminate in awareness as their result. And if awareness belonged to something other than the Self, that too would itself be the Self — non-composite, existing for its own sake, not for another's. Nor can we understand the body, senses, and objects as existing for their own sake, since we observe that their establishment depends on cognitions that terminate in awareness. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.105 //

body.text: nanu dehasyāvagatau na kaścit pratyakṣādipratyayāntaram apekṣate // SamUpad_II,2.106 //
body.translated_text: [Objection:] But for the body's awareness, no one requires any other cognition such as perception. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.106 //

body.text: bāḍham, jāgraty evaṃ syāt / mṛtisuṣuptyos tu dehasyāpi pratyakṣādipramāṇāpekṣayaiva siddhiḥ / tathaivendriyāṇām / bāhyā eva hi śabdādayo dehendriyākārapariṇatā iti pratyakṣādipramāṇāpekṣayaiva [hi] siddhiḥ / siddhir iti ca pramāṇaphalam avagatim avocāma, sā cāvagatiḥ kūṭasthā svayaṃsiddhātmajyotiḥsvarūpeti ca // SamUpad_II,2.107 //
body.translated_text: True, this would be so in the waking state. But in death and deep sleep, even the body's establishment depends on means of valid knowledge such as perception. The same is true of the senses. For external [objects] — sound and the like — are constituted in the form of the body and senses, together with the internal organ in its twofold form and its object-form, being mutually connected and composite in all activities. And we have said that establishment means awareness, which is the result of the means of valid knowledge; and that this awareness is immutable, self-established, and of the nature of the Self's own light. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.107 //

body.text: atrāha codakaḥ -- avagatiḥ pramāṇānāṃ phalaṃ kūṭasthanityātmajyotiḥsvarūpeti ca vipratiṣiddham / ity uktavantam āha -- na vipratiṣiddham / kathaṃ tarhi / kūṭasthanityāpi satī pratyakṣādipratyayānte lakṣyate, tādarthyāt / pratyakṣādipratyayasyānityatve 'nityeva bhavati / tena pramāṇānāṃ phalam ity upacaryate // SamUpad_II,2.108 //
body.translated_text: Here the objector says: 'Awareness is the result of the means of valid knowledge' and 'It is of the nature of immutable, eternal Self-light' — these are contradictory. To this the [teacher] says: They are not contradictory. How so? Though being immutable and eternal, [awareness] is perceived at the end of cognitions such as perception, since it is their purpose. When the cognition of perception and the like is non-eternal, [awareness appears to be] non-eternal. Therefore it is figuratively said to be the result of the means of valid knowledge. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.108 //

body.text: yady evaṃ bhagavan, kūṭasthanityāvagatir ātmajyatiḥsvarūpaiva svayaṃsiddhā, ātmani pramāṇanirapekṣatvāt, tato 'nyad acetanaṃ saṃhatyakāritvāt parārtham / yena ca sukhaduḥkhamohapratyayāvagatirūpeṇa pārārthyaṃ tenaiva svarūpeṇānātmano 'stitvaṃ nānyena rūpāntareṇa, ato nāstitvam eva paramārthataḥ / yathā hi loke rajjusarpamarīcyudakādīnāṃ tadavagativyatirekeṇābhāvo dṛṣṭaḥ, evaṃ jāgratsvapnadvaitabhāvasyāpi tadavagativyatirekeṇābhāvo yuktaḥ / evam eva, bhagavan, avagater ātmajyotiṣo nairantaryabhāvāt kūṭasthanityatā, advaitabhāvaś ca sarvapratyayabhedeṣv avyabhicārāt / pratyabhedās tv avagatiṃ vyabhicaranti / yathā svapne nīlapītādyākārabhedarūpāḥ pratyayās tadavagatiṃ vyabhicarantaḥ paramārthato na santīty ucyante, evaṃ jāgraty api nīlapītādipratyayabhedās tām evāvagatiṃ vyabhicaranto 'satyarūpā bhavitum arhanti / tasyāś cāvagater anyo 'vagantā nāstīti na svena svarūpeṇa svayam upādātuṃ hātuṃ vā śakyate, anyasya cābhāvāt // SamUpad_II,2.109 //
body.translated_text: [The disciple says:] If so, O blessed one, if immutable, eternal awareness is of the very nature of the Self's own light and self-established, independent of means of valid knowledge regarding the Self, then everything else, being unconscious and acting in combination, exists for another's sake. And that by which the non-Self's existence is [established] — namely through the form of awareness of cognitions of pleasure, pain, and delusion — by that very form alone is the non-Self's existence [known], and not by any other form; therefore, its non-existence is the ultimate truth. For just as in the world, the rope-snake, mirage-water, and the like are seen to be non-existent apart from the awareness of them, so too the duality of waking and dream is reasonably non-existent apart from the awareness of it. Just so, O blessed one, because awareness, the Self's own light, exists without interruption, it is immutable and eternal; and because it does not deviate in all the differences of cognitions, the state of non-duality [is established]. But the differences of cognitions deviate from awareness. Just as in dream, the cognitions that take the form of blue, yellow, and other shapes, deviating from the awareness [of them], are said to be ultimately non-existent, so too in waking, the differences of cognitions such as blue, yellow, and the like, deviating from that very awareness, ought to be of unreal form. And since there is no other knower of that awareness, it cannot be taken up or abandoned by itself through its own nature, and because there is no other [knower]. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.109 //

body.text: tathaiveti / eṣāvidyā, yannimittaḥ saṃsāro jāgratsvapnalakṣaṇaḥ / tasyā avidyāyā vidyā nivartikā / ityevaṃ tvam abhayaṃ prāpto 'si / nātaḥparaṃ jāgratsvapnaduḥkham anubhaviṣyasi, saṃsāraduḥkhān mukto 'sīti // SamUpad_II,2.110 //
body.translated_text: [The teacher says:] Just so. This is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), on account of which <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration), characterized by waking and dream, [proceeds]. <s>Vidyā</s> (knowledge) is the remover of that <s>avidyā</s>. Thus you have attained fearlessness. Henceforth you will not experience the suffering of waking and dream; you are liberated from the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s>. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.110 //

body.text: om iti // SamUpad_II,2.111 //
body.translated_text: <s>Om</s>. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2.111 //

body.text: iti avagatiprakaraṇam // SamUpad_II,2 //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the <s>Avagati-prakaraṇa</s> (Chapter on Awareness). // <s>SamUpad</s> II,2 //

body.text: mumukṣūṇām upāttapuṇyāpuṇyakṣapaṇaparāṇām apūrvānupacayārthināṃ parisaṃkhyānam idam ucyate / avidyāhetavo doṣā vāṅmanaṇkāyapravṛttihetavaḥ, pravṛtteś ceṣṭāniṣṭamiśraphalāni karmāṇy upacīyanta iti tanmokṣārtham // SamUpad_II,3.112 //
body.translated_text: This enumeration (<s>parisaṃkhyāna</s>) is stated for seekers of liberation who are intent upon exhausting accumulated merit and demerit and who seek the non-accumulation of new [<s>karma</s>]. The defects that are causes of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) are the causes of the activities of speech, mind, and body; and from activity, actions bearing pleasant, unpleasant, and mixed results accumulate — therefore, this [meditation] is for the purpose of liberation from that. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,3.112 //

body.text: tatra śabdasparśarūparasagandhānāṃ viṣayāṇāṃ śrotrādigrāhyatvāt svātmani pareṣu vā vijñānābhāvaḥ, teṣām eva pariṇatānāṃ yathā loṣṭādīnām / śrotrādidvāraiś ca jñāyante / yena ca jñāyante sa jñātṛtvād atajjātīyaḥ / te hi śabdādayo 'nyonyasaṃsargitvāj janmavṛddhi[vi]pariṇāmāpakṣayanāśasaṃyogaviyogāvirbhāvatirobhāvavikāravikārikṣetrabījādyanekadharmāṇaḥ, sāmānyena ca sukhaduḥkhādyanekadharmāṇaḥ / tadvijñātṛtvād eva tadvijñātā sarvaśabdādidharmavilakṣaṇaḥ // SamUpad_II,3.113 //
body.translated_text: Therein, since the sense-objects — sound, touch, form, taste, and smell — are apprehended by the ear and other [senses], there is no awareness in them by themselves or in others; they are like clods of earth and the like when transformed. And they are known through the doors of the ear and the like. And the one by whom they are known, being the knower, is of a different class from them. For sound and the like, being mutually connected, have numerous properties: birth, growth, transformation, decline, destruction, conjunction, disjunction, manifestation, disappearance, modification, the modified, field, seed, and so forth; and in general, numerous properties such as pleasure, pain, and the like. Because the knower of them knows them, the knower is entirely different in character from all the properties of sound and the like. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,3.113 //

body.text: tatra śabdādibhir upalabhyamānaiḥ pīḍyamāno vidvān evaṃ parisaṃcakṣīta // SamUpad_II,3.114 //
body.translated_text: Therein, being afflicted by the perceived [objects] of sound and the like, the wise person should reflect as follows: // <s>SamUpad</s> II,3.114 //

body.text: śabdas tu dhvanisāmānyamātreṇa viśeṣadharmair vā ṣaḍjādibhiḥ priyaiḥ, stutyādibhir iṣṭaiḥ, aniṣṭaiś cāsatyabībhatsaparibhavākrośādibhir vacanaiḥ, māṃ dṛksvabhāvam asaṃsargiṇam avikriyam acalam anidhanam abhayam atyantasūkṣmam aviṣayaṃ gocarīkṛtya spraṣṭuṃ naivārhaty asaṃsargitvād eva mama / ata eva na śabdanimittā hānir vṛddhir vā / ato māṃ kiṃ kariṣyati stutinindādipriyāpriyatvādilakṣaṇaḥ śabdaḥ / avivekinaṃ hi śabdam ātmatvena gataṃ priyaḥ śabdo vardhayed apriyaś ca kṣapayet, avivekitvān na tu mama vivekino vālāgramātram api kartum utsahata iti / evam eva sparśasāmānyena tadviśeṣaiś ca śītoṣṇamṛdukarkaśādijvarodaraśūlādilakṣaṇaiś cāpriyaiḥ, priyaiś ca kaiścic charīrasamavāyibhir bāhyāgantukanimittaiś ca, na mama kācid vikriyā vṛddhihānilakṣaṇā asparśatvāt kriyate, vyomna iva muṣṭighāṭādibhiḥ / tathā rūpasāmānyena tadviśeṣaiś ca priyāpriyaiḥ strīvyañjanādilakṣaṇaiḥ, arūpatvān na mama kācid dhānir vṛddhir vā kriyate / tathā rasasāmānyena tadviśeṣaiś ca [priyāpriyaiḥ] madhurāmlalavaṇakaṭutiktakaṣāyair mūḍhabuddhibhiḥ parigṛhītaiḥ, arasātmakasya na mama kācid dhānir vṛddhir vā kriyate / tathā gandhasāmānyena tadviśeṣaiḥ priyāpriyaiḥ puṣpādyanulepanādilakṣaṇaiḥ, agandhātmakasya na mama kācid dhānir vṛddhir vā kriyate / "aśabdam asparśam arūpam avyayaṃ tathārasaṃ nityam agandhavac ca yat" iti śruteḥ // SamUpad_II,3.115 //
body.translated_text: Sound, whether in its general nature as mere vibration, or with particular properties such as the pleasant [notes] of <s>ṣaḍja</s> and the like, or with desirable [utterances] such as praise and the like, or with undesirable utterances such as falsehood, the disgusting, contempt, abuse, and the like — it does not deserve to touch me, who am of the nature of seeing, non-associated, without modification, immovable, indestructible, fearless, supremely subtle, and beyond the objects of the senses — precisely because of my non-associability. Therefore, neither loss nor increase is caused to me by sound. So what can sound — characterized as pleasant or unpleasant through praise, blame, and the like — do to me? Pleasant sound might increase, and unpleasant sound might diminish, one who has unreflectively identified with sound; but because of non-discrimination, it is not able to do even a hair's-breadth to me, the discriminating one. In the same way, touch in its general nature and its particular forms — cold, heat, softness, hardness, fever, stomach-pain, and the like that are unpleasant, and some that are pleasant, whether inherent in the body or caused by external factors — no modification characterized by increase or decrease is produced in me, because I am intangible, just as fist-blows and the like [do nothing] to space. Likewise, form in its general nature and its particular forms, pleasant and unpleasant, characterized by feminine features and the like — no loss or increase is produced in me, because I am formless. Likewise, taste in its general nature and its particular forms — sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent — grasped by those of deluded understanding — no loss or increase is produced in me, whose nature is not of taste. Likewise, smell in its general nature and its particular forms, pleasant and unpleasant, characterized by flowers, ointments, and the like — no loss or increase is produced in me, whose nature is not of smell. As <s>Śruti</s> declares: 'That which is without sound, without touch, without form, imperishable, likewise without taste, eternal, without smell.' // <s>SamUpad</s> II,3.115 //

body.text: kiṃ ca ya eva bāhyaḥ śabdādayas te śarīrākāreṇa saṃsthitāḥ, tadgrāhakaiś ca śrotrādyākārair antaḥkaraṇadvayatadviṣayākāreṇa ca, anyonyasaṃsargitvāt saṃhatatvāc ca sarvakriyāsu / tatraivaṃ sati viduṣo mama na kaścic chatrur mitram udāsīno vāsti / tatra yadi [kaścin]mithyājñānābhimānena priyam apriyaṃ vā prayuyuṅkṣeta kriyāphalalakṣaṇam, tan mṛṣaiva prayuyuṅkṣati saḥ / tasyāviṣayatvān mama -- "avyakto 'yam acintyo 'yam" iti smṛteḥ / tathā [sarveṣāṃ] pañcānām api bhūtānām avikāryaḥ, aviṣayatvāt / "acchedyo 'yam adāhyo 'yam" iti smṛteḥ / yāpi śarīrendriyasaṃsthānamātram upalakṣya madbhaktānāṃ viparītānāṃ ca priyāpriyādiprayuyuṅkṣā, tajjā ca dharmādharmādiprāptiḥ, sā teṣām eva, na tu mayy ajare 'mṛte 'bhaye, "nainaṃ kṛtākṛte tapataḥ", "na karmaṇā vardhate no kanīyān", "sabāhyābhyantaro hy ajaḥ", "na lipyate lokaduḥkhena bāhyah" ityādiśrutismṛtibhyaḥ / anātmavastunaś cāsattvād iti paramo hetuḥ / ātmanaś cādvayatvaviṣayāṇi, dvayasyāsattvāt, yāni sarvāṇy upaniṣadvākyāni, vistaraśaḥ samīkṣitavyāni samīkṣitavyānīti // SamUpad_II,3.116 //
body.translated_text: Moreover, the very same external [objects] of sound and the like are constituted in the form of the body, together with the apprehenders in the form of the ear and the like, the internal organ in its twofold form and its object-form, being mutually connected and composite in all activities. This being so, I, the wise one, have no enemy, friend, or neutral person. And if someone, through false knowledge and conceit, should wish to apply to me something pleasant or unpleasant characterized as the result of action — he applies it falsely, because I am not its object — as <s>Smṛti</s> declares: 'This [Self] is unmanifest, this [Self] is inconceivable.' Likewise, [I am] not to be modified by any of the five elements, because I am not their object — as <s>Smṛti</s> declares: 'This [Self] cannot be cut, this [Self] cannot be burned.' And the desire to apply pleasant or unpleasant [things] to my devotees or to those opposed to me, perceiving merely the configuration of body and senses, and the resultant attainment of <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) — that belongs to them alone, not to me who am ageless, immortal, and fearless — as declared by <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s>: 'Actions done and undone do not torment him,' 'He does not grow through action, nor become less,' 'He is unborn, both inside and outside,' 'He is not stained by worldly suffering, being external [to it].' And the supreme reason is the non-existence of what is not the Self. And all the <s>Upaniṣad</s> statements that have as their subject-matter the non-duality of the Self — since duality is non-existent — should be thoroughly examined in detail; they should be thoroughly examined. // <s>SamUpad</s> II,3.116 //

body.text: iti parisaṃkhyānaprakaraṇam // SamUpad_II,3 //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the <s>Parisaṃkhyāna-prakaraṇa</s> (Chapter on Enumeration). // <s>SamUpad</s> II,3 //

body.text: iti śrīmatparamahaṃsaparivrājakācāryaśrīgovindabhagavatpādapūjyaśiṣyasya śrīśaṃkarabhagavataḥ kṛtiḥ sakalavedopaniṣatsāropadeśasāhasrī samāptā
body.translated_text: Thus is completed the <s>Upadeśasāhasrī</s>, the essence of all <s>Vedas</s> and <s>Upaniṣads</s>, the work of the blessed <s>Śaṃkara</s>, the revered disciple of the blessed <s>Govindabhagavatpāda</s>, the <s>Paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya</s> (Supreme Ascetic and Wandering Teacher).
